title: A Lecture on the Science of Sleep
description: Four recordings about sleep: a lecture, a tutorial about a research project, a radio interview about teenagers and a podcast with sleep tips.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · A lecture
parts.intro: You will hear part of a university lecture by Dr Lewis about sleep.

script.speaker: Dr Lewis
script.text: Good morning. Today we're going to look at something we all do but few of us understand: sleep. On average, we spend about a third of our lives asleep.

script.speaker: Dr Lewis
script.text: For a long time, scientists assumed that the brain simply switched off at night. We now know that's completely wrong. During sleep, the brain is extremely busy.

script.speaker: Dr Lewis
script.text: Sleep moves in cycles of roughly ninety minutes. Each cycle includes light sleep, deep sleep and a stage in which we dream, known as rapid eye movement sleep.

script.speaker: Dr Lewis
script.text: Deep sleep is when the body repairs itself. Muscles grow, and the immune system gets stronger. Dreaming sleep, on the other hand, seems to be important for memory and emotions.

script.speaker: Dr Lewis
script.text: A famous experiment illustrates this. Students who learned a list of words and then slept remembered far more the next day than students who stayed awake for the same period. It wasn't the time that mattered, it was the sleep.

script.speaker: Dr Lewis
script.text: Now, many people believe they can train themselves to need less sleep. The evidence suggests otherwise. Most adults need between seven and nine hours, and people who claim to manage on five usually perform worse, even if they don't notice it themselves.

script.speaker: Dr Lewis
script.text: That last point is worth remembering. Tired people are poor judges of how tired they are.

parts.title: Part 2 · A tutorial
parts.intro: You will hear a student, Linh, talking to her tutor, Dr Evans, about a research project.

script.speaker: Dr Evans
script.text: Come in, Linh. I've read your draft proposal on student sleep. Tell me about your idea.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Well, I want to survey students at our university about how late they stay up, and then compare that with their exam results.

script.speaker: Dr Evans
script.text: Interesting. How many students do you plan to ask?

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: At first I thought two hundred, but my friend says that's too ambitious for one term. Maybe I should aim for one hundred.

script.speaker: Dr Evans
script.text: I'd say one hundred and fifty, if you use an online form. That's realistic and still gives you reliable results.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: OK. My other worry is honesty. Students might say they sleep eight hours when really it's five.

script.speaker: Dr Evans
script.text: Exactly, that's the weak point of any survey. So I suggest you don't rely only on questionnaires. Ask volunteers to wear a simple sleep tracker for a week.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: I hadn't thought of that. But wouldn't it be expensive?

script.speaker: Dr Evans
script.text: The department has ten trackers you can borrow, free of charge. You'd just have to book them before the end of this month.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Perfect. And what about the deadline for the proposal?

script.speaker: Dr Evans
script.text: Friday the twelfth. Not the fifth, I know I said that earlier, but the date has been moved.

parts.title: Part 3 · A radio interview
parts.intro: You will hear a radio presenter, Minh, interviewing a sleep researcher, Dr Nguyen, about teenagers.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Joining me is Dr Nguyen, a sleep researcher. Dr Nguyen, why do teenagers seem to hate mornings?

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: It isn't laziness, Minh, though that's what many parents assume. During adolescence the body clock shifts. Teenagers naturally feel sleepy later in the evening and wake later in the morning, sometimes by two hours.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: So a seven o'clock alarm is hard for them.

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: Very. Some schools in other countries have moved their start time to half past eight or later, and the results were striking: better attendance, better marks, and fewer car accidents among older students.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: That sounds like an easy win. Why doesn't every school do it?

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: Practical reasons mostly. Bus timetables, parents' working hours, after-school sports. I sympathise, but I'd argue the health benefits outweigh the inconvenience.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: And what about phones? Surely they're part of the problem.

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: Partly. The light from screens can delay sleepiness, but honestly I think the content matters more than the light. A thrilling video or an argument with a friend keeps the mind active.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: So what's your advice for teenagers listening now?

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: Switch off the screen an hour before bed, keep the room cool and dark, and try to get up at roughly the same time at weekends. A big lie-in on Sunday confuses the body clock even more.

parts.title: Part 4 · A podcast
parts.intro: You will hear Nam, a student, talking on his podcast about how he improved his sleep.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Hello and welcome to The Tired Student. I'm Nam, and today I'm sharing three things I've learned after a very bad year of sleeping.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Number one: caffeine. I used to drink coffee at four in the afternoon and wonder why I was awake at midnight. Caffeine stays in your body for up to eight hours, so my afternoon coffee was still working when I went to bed. Now I stop at lunchtime.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Number two: routine. I used to think being spontaneous was exciting, so I went to bed whenever I felt like it. The result was that I felt tired all the time. When I started going to bed at eleven every night, even on Fridays, my energy changed within a fortnight.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Number three, and this one surprised me: the bedroom. I used to do my homework on my bed. Experts say that if you work where you sleep, your brain starts to link the bed with stress. I moved my desk to the corner and bought a cheap lamp, and it made a difference.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: What didn't work? Well, I tried counting sheep. Honestly, it's boring, and boredom isn't relaxing when you're worried about an exam. A short walk before bed worked much better.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: So that's it. Nothing revolutionary, just small changes. If you try only one, I'd say start with the coffee. And now, if you'll excuse me, I need a nap.
